summary: Describes a way to encrypt RTP header extensions and contributing sources, metadata that SRTP otherwise leaves unprotected. Earlier attempts saw limited deployment because of complexity, and this one aims to be simpler. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Even when the voice in a call is sealed, the labels on the package can be seen. This seals the labels too.

questions: how to encrypt rtp header extensions
subtitle: Cryptex encrypts RTP header extensions and contributing sources that SRTP leaves in the clear.

tldr.problem: SRTP encrypts only the RTP payload, so header extensions (including audio levels and extension identifiers) and contributing sources (CSRCs) stay visible to anyone on the path. The earlier fix, RFC 6904, saw little adoption.
tldr.mechanism: Cryptex negotiates one SDP attribute, a=cryptex, then marks encrypted packets with new 'defined by profile' values (0xC0DE and 0xC2DE) and extends the SRTP encrypted portion to cover the CSRCs and all header extension data.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3711. It leaves the first bytes of the RTP header, sequence number and SSRC readable, so existing tools and SRTP key scheduling keep working.

today: RFC 9335 is a Proposed Standard from January 2023 that updates RFC 3711. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem: Exposed RTP Metadata
sections.content:
The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP, RFC 3711) authenticates the whole RTP packet but encrypts only the payload. That was acceptable when header fields such as the timestamp held little sensitive data, and some fields (SSRC and sequence number) have to stay readable because they feed key scheduling.

RFC 9335 names three leaks. First, header extension values can be sensitive. RFC 6904 notes this, and per-packet sound levels are specifically called sensitive in their own RFCs. Second, the numeric identifiers of extensions can fingerprint the endpoint or application. Third, CSRCs can let an eavesdropper work out who spoke and when in an otherwise secure conference call.
sections.plainLanguage: Even with the message locked in a box, the stickers on the outside can say who is talking and what app they use. That is a leak.

sections.title: Why the Earlier Attempt Fell Short
sections.content:
RFC 6904 proposed encrypting header extension values in 2013 but, per this RFC, has not seen significant adoption. The RFC lists four problems.

  • It is complicated: encryption is negotiated per extension, which needs signaling logic and a complex SRTP transform. A bug in one popular implementation went undetected for five years.
  • It protects only the values, not the identifiers or lengths, and not the CSRCs.
  • Each extension must be offered both encrypted and unencrypted, doubling the count and pushing implementations past the 14-extension limit of one-byte headers in RFC 8285, so two-byte headers are needed, which some implementations handle poorly.
  • The mix of one-byte and two-byte forms adds extra bytes to each packet.

The goals follow: build on SRTP and RFC 8285, protect identifiers, lengths, values and CSRCs, keep signaling and the crypto transform simple, and stay compatible with unencrypted endpoints and existing RTP tooling. Encrypting more of the header, such as the CSRC count, was rejected because current tools could not parse the result.
sections.plainLanguage: The first lock was so fiddly that few people used it and it still left some labels showing. This one is meant to be easy enough that people will actually switch it on.

sections.title: Negotiating Cryptex in SDP
sections.content:
Support is signaled with a new SDP attribute, a=cryptex. It is a property attribute with no value, usable at session or media level (RFC 8866). Its presence in an offer or answer means the endpoint can receive Cryptex packets. After both sides have confirmed this, each sender may decide on its own, packet by packet, whether to use Cryptex.

With BUNDLE (RFC 9143), if a=cryptex is present for one media line it MUST be present for all RTP-based m= sections in the same bundle group. This lets the encrypted MID header extension be processed. The attribute is in the TRANSPORT multiplexing category. Later offers and answers MUST handle it the same way as the initial exchange.

Peers MAY negotiate both Cryptex and RFC 6904. If both are available it is RECOMMENDED to use Cryptex, unless there is a compelling reason, such as middleboxes that must read some extensions in the clear. A single packet MUST NOT use both.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides first say, in the call setup, 'I can open Cryptex envelopes.' After that, each side can choose to use them for any packet.

sections.title: Marking Encrypted Packets and Header Processing
sections.content:
RFC 8285 uses the 16-bit 'defined by profile' field to tell one-byte from two-byte extension framing. Cryptex adds two values so a receiver can tell a packet is encrypted: 0xC0DE replaces 0xBEDE for one-byte extensions, and 0xC2DE replaces 0x100 for two-byte extensions. With two-byte headers, extension identifier 256 MUST NOT be negotiated.

Sending. If the packet has CSRCs or any header extensions, the sender sets the tag to 0xC0DE or 0xC2DE, matching the framing, and then encrypts. If there are CSRCs but no extensions, the sender MUST append an empty extension block (the tag with a length of zero) and set the X bit to 1, so the receiver knows the CSRCs are encrypted. The mechanism MUST NOT be used with header extensions other than the RFC 8285 kind.

Receiving. The receiver checks the 'defined by profile' field. If it is not one of the Cryptex values, the packet is handled according to whichever specification defines that value. A receiver that requires Cryptex MUST stop processing and report an error. Otherwise it decrypts and passes the packet on.
sections.plainLanguage: A special stamp on the envelope says 'the labels inside are locked.' The receiver checks for the stamp before opening it.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
The procedure is the same as RFC 3711 except for what is covered by the Encrypted Portion. It MUST include the CSRC identifiers, the header extension data (everything after the first 4 bytes of the extension block) and the RTP payload. Those first 4 bytes, which hold the tag and length, stay unencrypted as RFC 8285 requires. The cipher input is the CSRCs, the extension data, the payload, then any padding and pad count.

The first 4 times CC bytes of ciphertext go back into the CSRC field, and the rest becomes the payload. For AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM, the 12-byte fixed header and the 4-byte extension header are the associated data. Because they are not contiguous when CSRCs are present, an implementation can swap the extension header and CSRC fields into an intermediate form for the cipher and swap them back afterwards. That form is for reference only and is never sent on the wire.

To keep code changes small, implementations can swap the 'defined by profile' value while encrypting or decrypting. The appendix provides test vectors for AES-CTR and AES-GCM across one-byte, two-byte, CSRC and empty-extension cases.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock now covers the extra labels too, but the first few bytes stay visible, like the front of the envelope, so the mail system can still sort it.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The first two bytes of the RTP packet are left unencrypted so systems that demultiplex on RTPv2 headers keep working. The sequence number and SSRC stay in the clear because SRTP key scheduling depends on them.

All security considerations from Section 9 of RFC 3711 apply, except Section 9.4, since confidentiality of the RTP header is the purpose here. The risks of weak or NULL authentication from Section 9.5 apply to encrypted header extensions as well. Cryptex does not change how SRTP authentication works, and since more of the packet is encrypted, the RFC calls this necessarily an improvement.

These fields remain unencrypted: RTP version, padding bit, extension bit, number of CSRCs, marker bit, payload type, sequence number, timestamp, SSRC identifier, and the number of header extensions. The RFC considers them low sensitivity. If any of them needed encryption, SRTP is likely the wrong protocol and a fully encapsulating one such as DTLS is preferred, at the cost of per-packet overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: A few facts must stay in view, like the street name on the parcel, so the postal system can work. Everything else the designers could safely hide is hidden.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC adds the SDP attribute cryptex to the attribute-name subregistry of the SDP Parameters registry. It takes no value, is usable at session and media level, is not charset dependent, and has the TRANSPORT mux category. Its purpose is to indicate that the endpoint can receive RTP packets encrypted with Cryptex. The contact is the IETF AVT Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The new setup word goes on the official list so nobody else uses the same word for something different.

items.title: Encrypted
items.text: CSRC identifiers, header extension data after the first 4 bytes, and the RTP payload.

items.title: Left readable
items.text: The fixed RTP header, the 4-byte extension header, and fields SRTP needs such as SSRC and sequence number.

items.title: Authenticated
items.text: The whole packet, as in SRTP; Cryptex does not change authentication.
